transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (CTO), Maya (NetEng), Sam (Cloud Eng), Anya (PM)
Shared links: redwood.com/sec-pack (shared), redwood.com/private-onramp-checklist (mention), spreadsheet: veridian-benchmark-template.xlsx (note)

[00:00] Alex (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for joining — really appreciate the time. quick rundown: i'm alex, i'm the AE, priya's our SE she'll run the bench plan later. could we quick go around and what you're hoping to get out of today?
[00:12] Jordan (Veridian - CTO): yeah thanks alex. i'm jordan. we're evaluating options to run our llm inference for product search and summarization. high level we want private connectivity, locked down data residency in eu-west-1, and predictable latency. primary ask is how we get redwood Private into our vpc with minimal egress exposure.
[00:28] Maya (NetEng): maya here — main constraints: no internet egress from pods, all traffic must go through our transit gateway, egress IPs need to be static for allowlist, and we'd like to avoid double-natting if possible.
[00:40] Sam (Cloud Eng): and sam: we'll need kms integration for key management and need to know whether token logs or payloads ever hit redwood controllers outside our region.
[00:52] Priya (Redwood SE): great context. quick note: we support Private (vpc-onramp) with customer-managed VPC peering, privatelink-style endpoints, and a private control plane option. there are tradeoffs — peering gives lower latency for high-throughput but requires routing updates, PrivateLink gives tighter security posture with interface endpoints but sometimes adds a slight latency delta.
[01:20] Jordan: we are leaning to peering since we have high throughput. but our compliance folks worry about cross-account routing and need proof of no egress to public internet. is that easy to demonstrate?
[01:33] Priya: yes — for Private we can operate in two models: 1) dedicated private dataplane inside your VPCs (we deploy data plane connectors into your accounts/regions) so traffic never leaves peered subnets, or 2) a managed transit setup where traffic routes to our service VPC over peering and we provide egress IPs you can allowlist. both can be audited. we have SOC2 artifacts and network flow examples — i'll share the packet flow diagram.
[02:03] Maya: when you say 'deploy into our account', do you create instances in our VPC? what's the footprint and permissions required?
[02:12] Priya: good q. typical pattern: we provide a terraform module to provision minimal infra — a few ENIs, an autoscaling group or EKS nodepool for the data-plane pods, and an IAM role with limited permissions (describe network, create interfaces, s3 access if you opt for object cache). the infra stays in your account; keys remain in your kms if you choose customer-managed keys. overhead is modest — depends on QPS and model size.
[02:43] Sam: that aligns with our ops model. on kms — will redwood ever hold plain-text data? for example, logs or payloads?
[02:52] Priya: in Private mode with customer-managed dataplane, payloads are processed within your VPC. our control plane still handles orchestration metadata, but we can configure it to not store request payloads and keep logs at a tokenized level. we also support envelope encryption with your KMS so you retain ultimate key control.
[03:17] Alex: just to add: for enterprise customers we offer contractual SLAs and an audit runbook for reviewers. we typically provide a security slide deck and example network ACLs.
[03:28] Jordan: excellent. two more constraints: 1) we have regional lock — everything must remain in eu-west-1, 2) some teams may want a disaster failover in us-east-1 but that's gated by compliance. can redwood run the data plane only in eu-west-1?
[03:45] Priya: yes. we can pin data-plane deployments to a single region. model artifacts can be cached in-region; fallback to other regions is possible but only with customer consent and config. we also support cross-region replication for model weights if you opt in.
[04:02] Maya: about egress — you've mentioned egress IPs. how many ip addresses do you need? our firewall team wants a small CIDR or static ip list.
[04:11] Priya: for managed egress we provide a small set of static NAT gateway IPs per deployment, typically a handful that scale with nodes. for peering-with-data-plane-in-account, egress isn't necessary because traffic never leaves your networks except to external services you call; in that model you control egress via your own NATs.
[04:34] Speaker 2 (auto-labeling error): mmm, can you also talk about kv cash?
[04:37] Priya: sure — KV cache (sometimes transcribed as kv cash) is an optimization; we maintain the kv cache inside the data-plane memory in your VPC so it doesn't traverse public networks.
[04:47] Jordan: latency numbers — we're aiming for p95 < 120ms for short prompts (~256 tokens) with batching. can you achieve that with peered dataplane?
[04:58] Priya: yes, we've gotten similar p95 numbers in peered private dataplane setups with optimized runtimes. exact depends on model (quantized vs fp16), instance types, and batch size. we'll run a lab bench to simulate your payloads — that'll give concrete numbers.
[05:18] Sam: speaking of instance types — do you support TPU/GPU variants or is it all gpu on aws g4/g5?
[05:25] Priya: for private deployments on aws we currently support accelerated GPU instances (g4/g5/p4 when available) and we have a bring-your-hardware option for on-prem. we don't yet support cloud tpu as a native offering.
[05:38] Anya (PM): question on autoscaling — will scaling cause ip churn that breaks our allowlist?
[05:45] Priya: if you use our managed egress we coordinate stable egress IPs via NATs. with in-account data-plane, all egress is under your control, so scaling doesn't change external egress ip footprint beyond your own NAT configuration.
[05:57] Maya: how do we integrate with our corporate SSO for access to the console and audit logs?
[06:03] Alex: we support SAML SSO and can map roles for admin/observer. audit logs can be exported to your cloud logging (cloudwatch / stackdriver) or shipped to your SIEM via our log-forwarder; note some logs are anonymized by default.
[06:21] Jordan: curious about network topology options — we prefer to avoid peering across a huge number of accounts. we use a transit hub. can redwood integrate via transit gateway attachment?
[06:32] Priya: yes — we can peer with a central service VPC and you can transit route to it via transit gateway or use interface endpoints. we typically recommend service VPC + transit for multi-account setups to minimize peering sprawl. downside: one extra hop, small latency bump, but much easier to manage at scale.
[06:54] Sam: any special port requirements or ipsec specifics? our security team enforces only TLS 1.3 and mutual TLS where possible.
[07:02] Priya: all control and data plane traffic uses mTLS and TLS 1.3. ports are standard https (443) for control plane; data plane uses internal service ports — we'll provide a port list. we can also support customer-managed ipsec tunnels if that's required by policy, though that's not the default.
[07:20] Jordan: what's the support model during onboarding — will we get an se assigned for the bench?
[07:25] Alex: yes, priya will run the benchmark and we assign a solutions engineer and an onboarding engineer for the first 90 days.
[07:33] Maya: we have some region gating — certain datasets cannot leave eu-west-1 and can't be backed up to other regions. how does your backup/metrics pipeline behave?
[07:43] Priya: metrics and metrics-only telemetry can be kept in-region. backups for model artifacts are configurable: we can keep caches and model weights in-region. telemetry that includes metadata can be routed to your monitoring account via log-forwarder. system-level backups are optional; we can disable cross-region snapshots by default.
[08:05] Anya: plan/ timeline — our procurement cycle needs a POC in January, procurement signoff by March. can redwood do a short pilot in mid-January?
[08:14] Alex: yes, that's realistic. we'll start by sharing security docs this week, propose bench dates for the week of Jan 10, and if bench results look good, pilot contract and reserved capacity talks after.
[08:26] Jordan: pricing — we have to justify cost vs our in-house inference and vs other vendors. can you provide an initial TCO for a 100 qps sustained workload?
[08:36] Alex: we'll put together a cost model comparing Hosted, Dedicated, and Private (in-account dataplane). it'll include instance costs, networking egress, and expected token costs. we'll add sample quantization/throughput tradeoffs.
[08:52] Priya: one note — with Private in-account dataplane you save on outbound egress because model traffic stays internal; with Hosted you typically see provider egress at normal public rates.
[09:04] Maya: anything around certificates and rotation — does your module integrate with our cert manager or do you manage certs?
[09:12] Priya: we can integrate with cert-manager (in-cluster) or you can use our managed certificates. for mTLS between control and data plane we accept customer-provided certs and rotation policies, so you stay in control.
[09:28] Jordan: curious about rollback and model version pinning — if we do canary and a model regresses, how do we fall back to a different variant automatically?
[09:37] Priya: our rollout system supports model pinning and canary rules. you can define percent rollouts, automatic rollback on increased error rates or quality regression triggers (we can wire in your eval hooks), and route-by-policy by latency or cost tiers.
[09:56] Alex: jumping in — competitor question: Jordan had asked about other vendors; our key difference is observability and cost controls for inference in production.
[10:06] Jordan: noted. one last nitty gritty — firewall needs ASN info and peering time windows. who will provide these?
[10:14] Priya: we'll provide ASN, peering ip ranges, BGP examples if you go that route, and an onboarding checklist.
[10:23] Sam: ok can we get specific on the lab bench — what telemetry and sample prompts do you need from us?
[10:29] Priya: sample prompts (prod-like), expected RPS/QPS, token length distribution, and whether you'll use streaming. we'll also need a representative model (or model family) and dataset for quality tests. we'll run latency and throughput sweeps and provide a spreadsheet with p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1k tokens.
[10:50] Anya: procurement will want a draft statement of work and a contract outline for private deployment — do you have a template?
[10:57] Alex: yes, we'll attach a draft SOW and standard enterprise addendum — i'll send with the security pack.
[11:05] Jordan: any limitations around EKS vs EC2? we predominantly run EKS.
[11:10] Priya: we support both; we provide helm/terraform for EKS and the runtime is containerized. we recommend nodegroups with gpu-optimized AMIs for best perf.
[11:20] Maya: if we go with peering to your service VPC, how are routes propagated to our subnets?
[11:26] Priya: you can use static routes or propagate via TGW. for many customers we give a helper script to program route tables based on peering attachments.
[11:34] Speaker label glitch (auto): [laughter]
[11:36] Priya: (laughs) — sorry, must be the transcription.
[11:40] Alex: let's do a quick recap and concrete next steps.
[11:43] Alex: Redwood will: share security pack + SOC2 links, propose benchmark dates (Priya), send draft SOW and pricing.
[11:52] Jordan: Veridian will: share network diagram, CIDR ranges, and compliance constraints; identify procurement lead.
[12:00] Maya: action - i'll collect firewall rules and give the small list of services we need allowed.
[12:07] Sam: i'll extract sample prompts and a small dataset for the bench.
[12:12] Anya: procurement timeline noted. we'll aim to confirm pilot by Jan 20.
[12:18] Alex: perfect. i'll send the pack today. any final questions?
[12:24] Jordan: none from me, thanks everyone.
[12:27] Priya: thanks all — we'll follow up with bench dates.
[12:30] Alex: thanks, meeting end.
